newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU transport network needs private input - Kinnock.
newsitem.headline: EU transport network needs private input - Kinnock.

text.p: European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock said on Tuesday that developing trans-European networks could benefit from partnerships between the public and private sectors.
Speaking at a European Research Centre conference on transport infrastructure, Kinnock said modern needs made it necessary to loosen a traditional bond between the state and transport sector funding.
"In this context, public/private financing partnerships could clearly be an important way of helping to accelerate the development of trans-European networks," he said.
The EU faces a huge bill to to develop trans-European transport infrastructure, with greatest emphasis on railways and then on road networks.
"As a rough estimate, the total investment needed for the trans-European network projects of common interest until 2010 is around 400 billion Ecu ($500 billion)," Kinnock said.

"Any private investment coming in alleviates the pressure on the public purse and the public money coming in underwrites what could be thought of as the political and procedural risks of involvement. That's why the partnership is a good idea," he told journalists after delivering his speech.
A mixture of public and private sector finance would help secure fresh investment as well as increasing the efficiency of implementing schemes, Kinnock said.

He said states would always have the responsibility to back transport projects that are efficient, although they had access to potentially cheaper funding than the private sector, which was wary of directly funding public infrastructure.

"It is vital, therefore, that ways are found to allow the private sector the scope to produce the increased efficiencies which will make investment in major infrastructure projects worthwhile," he told conference delegates.

Kinnock said he had set up a mixed group of EU transport ministers' representatives and private sector experts from finance, construction and management to identify and remove obstacles to public/private partnerships.
Asked his views about the funding history of troubled Anglo-French channel tunnel company Eurotunnel, Kinnock said it was a good example which proved the necessity of public and private partnership.
Eurotunnel on Monday announced a deal giving bank creditors 45.5 percent of the company in return for wiping out 1.0 billion stg ($1.6 billion) of its massive debts.

"The problem with the Channel Tunnel is that for ideological reasons 16 years ago, the government insisted that there be no public money. Many now acknowledge that had there been a public investment commitment in partnership... the passage of that critical piece of infrastructure would have been much smoother than it has been," he told journalists.
Unless action were taken on transport infrastructure, the future held the prospect of congestion and pollution, he said.

"Significant delay or failure to exploit new means of development and financing can only mean higher bills in the medium term and then, when the pressures make modernisation inevitable, higher costs," Kinnock said.
-- Keiron Henderson, Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000 ($ = 0.798 European Currency Unit ECUs) ($ = 0.640 British Pounds Sterling)
